transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-03
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Priya (NovusHealth CTO), Oliver (Platform Eng), Sandra (Security)
Shared artifacts: https://redwood.link/benchmark-template.xlsx, https://redwood.link/security-pack.pdf

Summary:
Quick scoping to align on benchmark success criteria, what customer scripts are required for the harness, streaming vs non-streaming trade-offs, and timeline for pilot handoff. Customer is in regulated healthcare; strong preference for private deployment later but wants hosted POC to validate throughput first.

Topics:
- Workload sizing (QPS, tokens per request, avg/session)
- Acceptance criteria (p99 latency, error rate, model quality thresholds)
- Harness integration (script format, auth, telemetry hooks)
- Streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for their UX
- Data/security (KMS, SOC2, SSO, redaction)
- Timeline and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: All right, hey everyone thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Priya: Priya here, hi.
[00:10] Oliver: Oliver.
[00:12] Sandra: Sandra.
[00:13] Ethan: Ethan from Redwood. Maya: me.
[00:16] Maya: Cool, uh Maya, so the agenda — we want to lock down the benchmark success criteria and the script handoff for the harness. Can you kick us off with current constraints Priya?
[00:28] Priya: Yeah, so short story — we're building a clinician-facing summarization service, expect bursts during morning rounding and then steady usage. Average prompt size is around 600 to 1,200 tokens, but some sessions have long transcripts up to 6k tokens. We need p99 latency to be under 500ms for short queries, and for long ones we accept up to 2.5s but want predictable tail behavior. Also, data residency: must be able to deploy in our V P C or on-prem later. For the POC though, we're OK with hosted as long as logs are segregated.
[00:58] Ethan: Got it. When you say p99 under 500ms for short queries — do you mean end-to-end including network?
[01:05] Priya: Yes, end-to-end from our app to the inference response.
[01:09] Oliver: To add, our peak concurrency target for the pilot is 120 concurrent sessions generating roughly 150 QPS with an average of 900 tokens per response. We can throttle clients but would like the system to handle that baseline for the POC.
[01:23] Maya: Okay that gives us a baseline. For the harness we'll need three things from you: sample customer scripts (anonymized), an API log sample for 72 hours, and your rate profile (burst/tps) — preferably CSV.
[01:35] Oliver: We'll prepare those. Question: how should we format the scripts? We have a mix of streaming and non-streaming clients.
[01:41] Ethan: Good question. Our benchmark harness accepts NDJSON with fields: request_id, timestamp, prompt, expected_token_count, and optionally stream=true/false. We also support a minimal websocket adapter for streaming. We'll share a sample adapter.
[01:55] Priya: Is there any requirement to change our client to use a Redwood SDK? We prefer not to refactor large parts of the app for the POC.
[02:02] Maya: No, not required. The harness runs externally and can replay via HTTP POSTs or via the websocket shim. For streaming we'll replay as chunked events — small change but doable on your side.
[02:12] Sandra: From security, we need to know how logs are handled. Does Redwood persist raw prompts? We have PHI and need strict redaction.
[02:19] Ethan: By default hosted POC will persist anonymized telemetry only; raw prompt retention is configurable. For the dedicated/private path you can opt out of prompt retention entirely. We integrate with customer K M S for key management if on Private.
[02:31] Sandra: Okay please include that in the security pack. Also SOC two and ISO controls?
[02:35] Maya: We'll attach SOC 2 Type II evidence and our ISO faq in the security-pack.pdf link.
[02:40] Oliver: Back to workload sizes — you mentioned KV cache earlier in docs. Does Redwood warm the K V cache across sessions for the POC?
[02:47] Ethan: We can enable prefix/K V cache warmups in the runtime. For the harness we typically run a warmup phase where we replay representative sessions 30–45 minutes before main load to populate the KV and prefix caches so cold-starts don't skew results. That will be part of the runbook I send.
[03:02] Priya: Nice. We want the benchmark to capture both cold starts and warmed scenarios. So acceptance criteria should specify both.
[03:08] Maya: Agreed. Proposal: acceptance gates — cold-start p95 under 1.5s for 6k-token sessions; warmed p99 under 2.5s for long sessions, short-query end-to-end p99 under 500ms with error <0.5%. Also quality regression: BLEU/ROUGE-style checks on a fixed eval set, and we can add a human review drop threshold.
[03:28] Priya: That sounds reasonable. For quality checks we mostly care about hallucination rate — we can provide some labeled prompts.
[03:34] Maya: Perfect. We'll include a metric for hallucination: <2% on your labeled set.
[03:38] Oliver: On streaming vs non-streaming what has been your experience? We have a mix of web UIs where progressive tokens improve perceived latency.
[03:45] Ethan: Streaming benefits perceived latency and reduces time-to-first-token but increases complexity in the harness. For throughput-focused tests, non-streaming (batch) is easier to measure and gives slightly better aggregate throughput because of fewer bookkeeping messages. For your UX where clinicians need early tokens, we recommend mixed-mode: stream first 128 tokens, then switch to non-stream for the remainder. The benchmark harness can simulate that pattern.
[04:10] Sandra: Are there implications for cost with streaming?
[04:12] Ethan: Minimal — streaming itself doesn't materially change GPU utilization, it's more about the per-connection overhead. But more sessions with many open streams increases memory/connection counts on the runtime, so we'll measure resource utilization and give a cost estimate.
[04:25] Maya: We'll include a cost/throughput sensitivity table in the preliminary estimate.
[04:29] Priya: Timeline — We're aiming to start the pilot runs in two weeks. Is that doable?
[04:33] Ethan: Two weeks is tight but doable if we get the scripts and logs within a week. The typical sequence: artifact handoff (1–3 days), Redwood harness adapter + warmup plan (2–3 days), dry run (1 day), full benchmark (1 day), then results review.
[04:48] Oliver: So realistically two weeks. Good. 
[04:50] Maya: We'll also need to agree on the pilot scope: model variant, quantization profile, and routing policy. For the POC we suggest starting with a 7B quantized variant and a fallback to a 13B if quality fails.
[05:02] Priya: We need to know the expected latency delta between the variants.
[05:06] Ethan: Roughly, 7B quantized should have 30–50% lower cost and about 20–30% lower latency for mid-length responses. We'll include benchmarked numbers from similar workloads in the shared spreadsheet.
[05:18] Priya: Ok. Also, for audit purposes we need per-request tracing and token-level cost breakdown.
[05:24] Maya: Redwood Console provides per-token cost and per-route latency traces. We'll give you a read-only access to the console for the pilot.
[05:31] Sandra: Make sure RBAC can be scoped for NovusHealth. We have separate roles for dev and compliance.
[05:36] Ethan: RBAC is available — we'll document role creation steps.
[05:40] Maya: Recap — deliverables and owners are in the action items. Next step is file exchange: benchmark-template.xlsx and security-pack.pdf go out by Monday, 2025-10-06. Handoff of scripts + traffic by 2025-10-10. Pilot run week of 2025-10-13.
[05:58] Priya: Sounds good. One last question — if we hit unexpected tail latencies during the pilot can Redwood do live routing to a higher tier to keep service stable?
[06:05] Ethan: Yes — we can configure routing policies and automatic fallback to a dedicated variant or a region with spare capacity. We'll exercise that in the runbook.
[06:12] Oliver: Great. We'll get the artifacts together. Thanks everyone.
[06:15] Maya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the files and calendar invite for the runbook workshop.
[06:20] (call ends)

Notes: transcription imperfect in spots — speaker overlaps and acronyms sometimes split (V P C, K V cache). See attached artifacts for exact schema.

End of transcript.
